summary: Long one of the world's hardest countries to visit, Equatorial Guinea still routes most nationalities through its embassies, although an official eVisa introduced in 2024 is starting to ease access. US citizens enjoy a rare visa-free bilateral arrangement, and CEMAC neighbors enter freely.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required if you arrive from a country with risk of transmission, and vaccination is recommended for all travelers — officials frequently ask for the yellow card regardless of routing.

source.name: Embassy of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea in Washington, D.C.

travelInsurance.text: Not a formal entry condition, but medical facilities are limited and insurance with evacuation coverage is strongly recommended.

source.name: Embassy of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea in Washington, D.C.

onwardTicket.text: Carry a return or onward ticket and proof of accommodation — immigration officers ask for both, and visa applications require them.

source.name: Embassy of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea in Washington, D.C.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; officers may ask visitors to show sufficient means, and visa applications typically require bank statements.

source.name: Embassy of the Republic of Equatorial Guinea in Washington, D.C.

notes: Photography of the presidential palace, ports, airports, military sites and government buildings is prohibited — cameras and phones can be seized.
Export of significant amounts of CFA francs and of wildlife products is restricted.

payments.text: Cash in CFA francs covers almost everything. Cards are accepted only at the few international hotels in Malabo and Bata, and ATMs are unreliable. Bring euros or US dollars to exchange.

safety.text: Violent crime is comparatively rare, but travelers face frequent police checkpoints, document checks and occasional petty extortion; photography rules are strictly enforced. Carry certified copies of your passport and visa at all times.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Equatorial Guinea travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to February is the driest, most comfortable window on Bioko island (Malabo) and pleasant on the mainland; rain falls year-round, peaking around April–May and October.

tips.text: US citizens are a striking exception to Equatorial Guinea's strict visa regime. They enter visa-free for short stays under a bilateral arrangement dating back decades. Every other Western nationality should plan on a visa.

Do not photograph the presidential palace, airports, ports, checkpoints or anything military or governmental. The rules are enforced and cameras or phones can be confiscated; ask permission before photographing people.
Carry your passport (or a certified copy) and visa at all times — police checkpoints are frequent on Bioko and the mainland, and missing documents commonly lead to fines or lengthy delays.

An official eVisa was introduced in 2024 and is gradually easing what was once one of the world's hardest tourist visas, but confirm the current application channel with an Equatoguinean embassy before relying on it, and avoid unofficial visa websites.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Equatorial Guinea?
faq.answer: Most nationalities do — historically via an embassy, though an official eVisa introduced in 2024 is easing access. The exceptions are US citizens, who enter visa-free under a bilateral arrangement, and CEMAC citizens (Cameroon, Chad, CAR, Congo, Gabon), who move freely.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Equatorial Guinea?
faq.answer: No — US passport holders enter visa-free for short tourist or business stays, commonly cited as up to 90 days, one of the very few such arrangements Equatorial Guinea maintains. Carry an onward ticket and, if arriving from a yellow fever risk country, your vaccination certificate.

faq.question: Does Equatorial Guinea have an eVisa?
faq.answer: Yes. An online eVisa was introduced in 2024 and is gradually rolling out for tourist visits. Coverage and eligibility are still settling, so confirm the current official application channel with an Equatoguinean embassy before you rely on it.

faq.question: Is Equatorial Guinea really that hard to visit?
faq.answer: It was long ranked among the world's most difficult destinations — few embassies, demanding paperwork and discretionary refusals. The 2024 eVisa is changing that, but expect more documentation than usual (hotel booking, bank statements, sometimes police clearance) and allow plenty of time.

faq.question: Is Equatorial Guinea safe for travelers?
faq.answer: Broadly yes in terms of crime, which is low by regional standards. The friction points are bureaucratic: frequent police checkpoints, strict photography rules and document checks. Keep your papers on you, avoid photographing anything official, and travel patiently.
